issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint filed by the Directorate of Enforcement under Section 44(1)(b) of the PMLA, 2002 was liable to be challenged on the ground that apart from s. 120B of the Indian Penal Code, no other offences were scheduled offences under the PMLA.

facts: The Directorate of Enforcement filed a complaint under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002.
The complaint was based on alleged offences under the Income-tax Act, 1961, and various sections of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
It was undisputed that out of all the alleged offences, only Section 120B of the IPC (criminal conspiracy) was a scheduled offence under the PMLA.
The other offences, which were the subject of the alleged conspiracy, were not listed in the PMLA Schedule.
law: The Court relied on the principle that the offence of criminal conspiracy under Section 120B of the IPC can only be considered a 'scheduled offence' if the conspiracy is to commit an offence that is itself specifically included in the Schedule to the PMLA.
An offence of money laundering under Section 3 of the PMLA requires the existence of 'proceeds of crime', which can only be generated from a 'scheduled offence'.
application: The Court applied the legal principle to the facts of the case, noting that the alleged conspiracy was to commit offences (under the Income-tax Act and other IPC sections) that were not scheduled offences.

Because the object of the conspiracy was not a scheduled offence, the charge of conspiracy under Section 120B could not, by itself, be treated as a scheduled offence for the purpose of the PMLA proceedings.
The Court reasoned that since no scheduled offence was made out in the complaint, there could be no 'proceeds of crime'.
Consequently, without proceeds of crime, an offence of money laundering under Section 3 of the PMLA could not be established.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the challenge, concluding that the complaint did not disclose any scheduled offence as defined by the PMLA. Since the conspiracy was to commit non-scheduled offences, the entire basis for the PMLA case was invalid. Accordingly, the Court quashed the complaint.

issue.issue_text: Whether the issue of the appellant having used tainted money forming part of the proceeds of crime for acquiring a property can be decided only at the time of trial.

facts: The appellant was accused of acquiring a property using 'tainted money', which was alleged to be the proceeds of a crime under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA).
The appellant made several submissions to the court, one of which was that the issue of the money's origin could only be decided at trial.
law: The legal question before the court was to determine the appropriate stage in the legal process to decide a factual issue, specifically whether a property was purchased with the proceeds of a crime.
application: The Supreme Court explicitly stated its conclusions after considering the appellant's submissions.
The Court noted that while it rejected the first and second submissions made by the appellant, the third submission "must be upheld."

The text directly quotes one of the Court's conclusions: "The issue of whether the appellant has used tainted money forming part of the proceeds of crime for acquiring the second property can be decided only at the time of trial."
This indicates that the court found the question to be a matter of fact that requires evidence and examination, which is the purpose of a trial, rather than a preliminary hearing.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the factual question of whether the appellant used proceeds of a crime to acquire a property is a matter that can only be properly determined during a full trial, and not at a preliminary stage. Therefore, it accepted the appellant's submission on this issue.

cases.case_name: Pavana Dibbur v. Directorate of Enforcement
cases.principle: In the absence of a scheduled offence, there cannot be any 'proceeds of crime'. If there are no proceeds of crime, the offence under Section 3 of the PMLA is not made out, as the existence of proceeds of crime is a condition precedent for the applicability of Section 3.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A property cannot be considered to be connected with the proceeds of a crime if the acts constituting the scheduled offense were committed after the property was acquired.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A complaint under the PMLA cannot be sustained if the underlying offences are not 'scheduled offences' as defined by the Act. The existence of 'proceeds of crime' is a mandatory condition precedent for an offence under Section 3 of the PMLA, and proceeds of crime can only be generated from a scheduled offence. In the absence of a scheduled offence, there can be no proceeds of crime, and therefore, no offence of money laundering is made out.
legal_tests_applied: The existence of 'proceeds of crime' is a condition precedent for the applicability of Section 3 of the PMLA. If there are no proceeds of crime, the offence under Section 3 is not made out.

In the absence of a scheduled offence, there cannot be any proceeds of crime within the meaning of clause (u) of sub-Section (1) of Section 2 of the PMLA, as established in Pavana Dibbur v. Directorate of Enforcement.
